This connects the tables together by pairing one line in a table with each line in the other table (Cartesian Product). To limit the number of rows returned, you should use the "ON" statement. This returns only lines in which the condition is specified after the statement is true, this is usually an equivalent operator with primary keys. You can also use the "THERE" statement to specify that only rows with column values that specify a specific condition should be returned. The "GROUP BY" statement groups rows with the same column values for which columns follow the statement. The "HAVING" statement will return groups that determine each condition that follows the statement. Each column(s) returned from grouped rows shall be either an aggregated function (AVG, MAX, COUNT, SUM, ...) of a column or the column(s) after which the data were grouped. To sort the returned data, you can use the ORDER BY command, which follows the data according to which aggregated function or column of the statement. The "DESC" statement will be sorted in descending order and the "ASC" statement will be sorted in ascending order. Finally, you can use the "LIMIT" statement to return a certain number of lines. If "*" is used in an SQL statement, each column is returned. For example, SELECT * FROM Table WO Attribute = 1 will select each column from rows with the attribute column equal to 1.

Value: This refers to a sentence that contains value judgments without making specific claims about what should be done (if so, then it is a policy sentence.). Fact: This refers to an objective sentence that expresses or treats facts or conditions without distortion by personal feelings, prejudices or interpretations. A fact set has a truth value that can be verified with objective evidence that may be available at the time of the claim; future forecasts are considered unverifiable. Testimony: This refers to an objective sentence about the author's personal condition or experience. Evidence of certificates is not publicly available in most cases.

task869_cfq_mcd1_sql_to_explanation.de: Determine whether the provided SQL statement addresses the specified question correctly. Output 1, if the SQL statement is correct and 0 is different. Each table has a primary key that uniquely identifies each line, usually an ID. To select which columns are returned, specify this according to the "SELECT" statement. Next, use a "FROM" statement to determine from which tables you want to select the data. If you specify a table, you can rename it with the "AS" statement. You can refer this table with any name that follows the "AS" statement. If you want to select data from multiple tables, you must use the "JOIN" statement. This connects the tables together by pairing one line in a table with each line in the other table (Cartesian Product). To limit the number of rows returned, you should use the "ON" statement. This returns only lines in which the condition is specified after the statement is true, this is usually an equivalent operator with primary keys. You can also use the "THERE" statement to specify that only rows with column values that specify a specific condition should be returned. The "GROUP BY" statement groups rows with the same column values for which columns follow the statement. The "HAVING" statement will return groups that determine each condition that follows the statement. Each column(s) returned from grouped rows shall be either an aggregated function (AVG, MAX, COUNT, SUM, ...) of a column or the column(s) after which the data were grouped. To sort the returned data, you can use the ORDER BY command, which follows the data according to which aggregated function or column of the statement. The "DESC" statement will be sorted in descending order and the "ASC" statement will be sorted in ascending order. Finally, you can use the "LIMIT" statement to return a certain number of lines. If "*" is used in an SQL statement, each column is returned. For example, SELECT * FROM Table WO Attribute = 1 will select each column from rows with the attribute column equal to 1.
